title: Turkmen v. Hasty (Second Circuit merits)
lead: Men detained on immigration charges after September 11 alleged discriminatory confinement and abuse. The Second Circuit allowed several damages claims against senior officials and jail administrators to proceed, carefully dividing claims by defendant; the Supreme Court later rejected much of that remedy analysis.

actors.name: John Ashcroft, Robert Mueller, and James Ziglar
actors.role: Attorney General, FBI Director, and immigration commissioner sued over policy

actors.name: Dennis Hasty, Michael Zenk, and James Sherman
actors.role: Metropolitan Detention Center wardens and associate warden

actors.name: Judge Raggi
actors.role: Judge partly concurring and partly dissenting

proceedings: After a fourth amended complaint, the district court dismissed the high-level officials and retained several jail-official claims. The Second Circuit affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded on June 17, 2015. Later Supreme Court review in Ziglar v. Abbasi reversed most of that judgment and vacated the remaining abuse-claim portion.
limits: These were pleading and immunity rulings, not findings of abuse or a damages award. The historical Second Circuit Bivens authorization was substantially rejected in Abbasi. Interference-with-counsel dismissals were not appealed.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: An immigration investigation led to restrictive detention
sections.cue: Introduce the detainees and distinguish official conditions from alleged abuse.
paragraphs: After September 11, 2001, eight men from the Middle East, North Africa, or South Asia were arrested on immigration charges. Six were Muslim, one Hindu, and one Buddhist. Six were held in Brooklyn’s Metropolitan Detention Center; Ibrahim Turkmen and Akhil Sachdeva were held at the Passaic County Jail. Their individual detentions generally lasted three to eight months. They challenged conditions and discriminatory treatment, not the proposition that immigration detention could ever be lawful.

The government initially held investigation detainees until the Federal Bureau of Investigation, or FBI, cleared terrorism connections. The New York FBI maintained a list that included people encountered through leads generating no individualized terrorism suspicion. The complaint alleged that actual or perceived race, religion, and national origin nevertheless determined severe restrictions.

At the Metropolitan Detention Center’s Administrative Maximum Special Housing Unit, alleged official conditions included twenty-three-hour confinement, constant light, shackles and extensive escorts outside cells, restricted communication, and repeated strip searches. Separate allegations described guards’ physical attacks, religious insults, threats, and obstruction of complaints. Official restrictions and unofficial abuse presented different questions of responsibility. These remained allegations accepted for dismissal review, not trial findings.

sections.title: The amended complaint connected the conditions to particular officials
sections.cue: Trace the parties and procedural route.
paragraphs: The defendants included former Attorney General John Ashcroft, FBI Director Robert Mueller, and Immigration and Naturalization Service Commissioner James Ziglar, referred to as the Department of Justice defendants. Jail officials included wardens Dennis Hasty and Michael Zenk and Associate Warden James Sherman. Captain Salvatore Lopresti and Lieutenant Joseph Cuciti also appeared; Cuciti did not appeal, and Lopresti’s appeal was dismissed for failure to pay a fee and file a brief.

The suit began in 2002. Earlier plaintiffs settled or withdrew, leaving Turkmen and Sachdeva, and six Metropolitan Detention Center detainees intervened. Following Ashcroft v. Iqbal, the Supreme Court pleading decision requiring plausible allegations of each official’s own misconduct, plaintiffs filed a fourth amended complaint informed by two Justice Department Inspector General reports unavailable at the outset.

The district court dismissed all claims against the Department of Justice defendants but retained several against jail officials. Those officials appealed; plaintiffs cross-appealed under a Rule 54(b) judgment. Plaintiffs did not appeal dismissal of their interference-with-counsel claims, numbered four and five.

sections.title: The majority separated remedy, plausibility, and immunity
sections.cue: Explain the threshold decisions before the individual claims.
paragraphs: Judges Pooler and Wesley distinguished whether Bivens, the precedent recognizing some implied constitutional damages actions against federal officers, supplied a remedy; whether each official’s own misconduct was plausibly alleged; and whether qualified immunity nevertheless barred suit. Supervisory rank alone was insufficient. But deliberate indifference or supervisory conduct could satisfy a particular constitutional wrong without becoming forbidden vicarious liability.

Plaintiffs incorporated the Inspector General reports except where their allegations contradicted them. The court could consider their language and context but could not resolve conflicting accounts as though after an evidentiary hearing.

The majority treated Fifth Amendment punitive-confinement and discrimination claims and Fourth Amendment strip searches as existing Bivens contexts because both the rights and injury mechanisms had previously appeared. The extraordinary emergency and asserted motive did not transform familiar confinement claims into new contexts. It therefore expressly did not reach alternative-remedy or special-factors analysis.

Free exercise under the First Amendment was different: the Supreme Court had recognized no such damages remedy, and the majority declined to create it without guidance. That claim failed against everyone.

sections.title: Punitive conditions plausibly involved some officials personally
sections.cue: Give the high-level and jail-specific allegations.
paragraphs: Under Bell v. Wolfish, the precedent governing punishment of pretrial detainees, restrictions lacking a reasonable relationship to legitimate objectives could support inferred punitive intent. The parties used that standard; the court reserved whether civil immigration detainees deserved greater protection. It did not require individualized terrorism suspicion for every ordinary detention restriction, but distinguished the extreme conditions alleged here.

High-level officials could initially expect lawful implementation of a lawful detention policy. The majority nonetheless found a plausible inference that the Department of Justice defendants endorsed continued extreme conditions after learning that detainees lacked suspected terrorism connections. It focused on the November 2001 merger of the New York and national immigration lists and allegations about information passing among officials. The merger theory was the court’s reading, not a theory plaintiffs had advanced in their briefs. The security explanation did not compel dismissal, although discovery might negate personal responsibility. The circuit’s prior Iqbal v. Hasty reasoning also supported denial of qualified immunity.

Hasty allegedly directed design of the jail conditions, which he and Sherman approved and implemented. Updates allegedly disclosed no terrorism evidence; required assessments were omitted, and officials approved a false representation that individualized high-security assessments had occurred. Benamar Benatta allegedly received clearance on November 14, 2001, but remained in the unit until April 30, 2002, with clearance information available to the jail.
Those allegations tied Hasty and Sherman personally to official conditions. General allegations against Zenk, who became warden April 22, 2002, when only two plaintiffs remained, did not.

sections.title: Unofficial abuse required a separate showing
sections.cue: Explain why Hasty and Sherman differed.
paragraphs: The unofficial-abuse claim required deliberate indifference to a serious risk. Hasty allegedly obstructed grievances, avoided rounds to avoid seeing abuse, learned of it through complaints, hunger strikes, and suicide attempts, and allowed it to continue. That pleaded his own indifference rather than liability merely from office.

Sherman’s alleged awareness was too vague to connect him adequately to unofficial abuse, and Zenk was not alleged responsible for it. Hasty therefore faced both official-conditions and unofficial-abuse claims; Sherman faced only official conditions. The majority denied qualified immunity on the surviving claims.

sections.title: Discrimination, searches, and conspiracy followed their own elements
paragraphs: Equal protection required purposeful discrimination, not knowledge of consequences alone. The majority found detailed allegations linking the merger decision and Hasty and Sherman’s conduct to discriminatory designations, distinguishing Iqbal’s more conclusory pleading. That many Arab or Muslim detainees went to less restrictive Passaic confinement did not compel dismissal because officials allegedly deferred to discriminatory designations and placement choices. Zenk’s allegations and the Passaic plaintiffs’ challenged-discrimination allegations were insufficient. Qualified immunity did not bar the surviving claims.

The search claim alleged repeated strip searches despite no opportunity to acquire contraband. Hasty and Sherman allegedly created and implemented the restrictions; logs added context rather than supplying the sole attribution. Using the parties’ rational-relationship standard, the majority found no legitimate prison purpose sufficiently established to dismiss or grant immunity. It reserved greater protection for civil detainees and dismissed Zenk for deficient allegations.

The separate 42 U.S.C. section 1985(3) claim required an agreement to deny equal protection, an act furthering it, injury or deprivation, and discriminatory animus. The merger, continued treatment, and false assessments supported coordinated conduct by the senior officials, Hasty, and Sherman. The intracorporate-conspiracy doctrine can treat one entity’s agents as unable to conspire, but varied responsibilities and separate policymaking prevented finding a single policymaking entity on these pleadings. Justice Department supervision of prisons did not settle that issue. The majority also rejected immunity under circuit precedent; Zenk’s and the Passaic plaintiffs’ conspiracy claims failed.

sections.title: Raggi would dismiss the surviving policy challenges
sections.cue: Explain her independent remedy and immunity objections.
paragraphs: Judge Raggi’s disagreement excluded the non-policy unofficial-abuse claims. For policy challenges, she defined the Bivens context through the full setting: immigration, national security, senior officers, and an unprecedented emergency. Combining a familiar right with a broadly described mechanism did not reproduce the cases Bivens, Davis, or Carlson. Separation of powers, executive responsibilities, congressional action and inaction, and possible prospective relief counseled against creating damages remedies. An alternative could matter without equivalent monetary compensation.

She also found plausibility and immunity deficient. The Inspector General attributed the list merger to Stuart Levey, not the named senior defendants; consultation with Ashcroft was speculative. Merger did not establish knowledge or intent about specific jail conditions. National security was the obvious, more likely explanation, and no precedent clearly required individualized terrorism suspicion for restrictive confinement in this emergency. An abstract prohibition on punishment did not resolve that specific question.

Raggi found discrimination insufficiently pleaded under Iqbal, especially given Passaic’s treatment of many Arab or Muslim detainees. For searches, she disputed personal responsibility and the premise that repetition necessarily lacked a rational security connection; a 2004 juvenile-search decision could not establish officials’ knowledge in 2001. Without equal protection, conspiracy failed too. Her proposed dismissal rested on remedy limits and independently immunity, not findings validating alleged acts after trial.

sections.title: The mixed judgment allowed litigation, not recovery
sections.cue: State the disposition and later change in governing analysis.
paragraphs: The Second Circuit affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded. For the Metropolitan Detention Center plaintiffs it reinstated senior officials’ punitive-confinement, discrimination, and conspiracy claims; permitted Hasty’s official-conditions, unofficial-abuse, discrimination, search, and conspiracy claims; and permitted corresponding Sherman claims except unofficial abuse. It dismissed free exercise universally, all Zenk claims, and the Passaic plaintiffs’ claims. No damages were awarded.

Later, in Ziglar v. Abbasi, the Supreme Court reversed the appellate judgment except Hasty’s prisoner-abuse claim, vacated that portion, and remanded. It rejected the broad Bivens-context analysis rather than resolving everything simply as implausible pleading. The 2015 ruling therefore describes a historical stage, not current authorization of these damages claims.
